title: Why the UK is thinking of rejoining UNIDO
label: 15 September 2026 · UNIDO evidence session
summary: Witnesses from the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero explained why the UK is considering rejoining the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), what reforms have happened there, how membership could help UK aims and developing countries, the challenge of getting climate money to the poorest, and how the UK would guard against backsliding — with a planned UK review in 2029.

speakers.label: Matt Toombs
speakers.name: Matt Toombs
speakers.role: Director for International Net Zero - Climate Finance and Strategy, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

speakers.label: Paul Durrant
speakers.name: Paul Durrant
speakers.role: Head of International Green Industrialisation, Technology Innovation & Electrification (IGNITE), Department for Energy Security and Net Zero

chapters.title: Why now: a changed context
chapters.takeaway: The UK thinks the world and its relationship with UNIDO have changed since 2012, so rejoining could be useful now.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Welcome. Our first big question: why should the UK rejoin UNIDO — the UN agency for industrial development — after leaving in 2012?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: The short answer is the context's different. Back in 2012 we had only a thin relationship. Since then we've worked with UNIDO on big programmes and built a deeper partnership.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Industrial development — especially 'green' or low-carbon industrial growth — matters for developing countries' jobs and economies, and it matters for global climate goals.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: If the UK wants to help shape that process, win contracts for UK businesses and mobilise finance, being inside UNIDO gives us more influence than being outside.

chapters.title: Examples of existing UK–UNIDO work
chapters.takeaway: The UK already works closely with UNIDO on several projects, giving practical reasons to rejoin.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: Can you give concrete examples where our engagement has mattered?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Yes. We worked with UNIDO through COP26 — that's the UN climate talks — and on green public procurement with India to boost demand for clean steel and concrete.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: There's an Accelerate-to-Demonstrate programme around £125 million. Also, UK work in Brazil — about £15 million of UK investment — has unlocked larger international and private finance.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Those examples show small UK sums can be used to leverage much larger funding and real jobs on the ground.

chapters.title: Have real reforms happened at UNIDO?
chapters.takeaway: UNIDO says it has become smaller, more transparent and has independent evaluation — the UK believes these are genuine improvements.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: When we left in 2012 there were governance problems. What reforms have actually happened?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: UNIDO has changed: it's leaner, publishes more about programme effectiveness, and has an independent evaluation unit. That's a clearer accountability picture than before.

turns.speaker: Baroness Anelay of St Johns
turns.text: Other countries left too. Have you talked to them about coming back?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We talk with like-minded countries but can't speak for them. Many industrialised countries — Japan, Italy, Germany and the EU — stayed involved, so the UK wouldn't be unusual in rejoining.

chapters.title: Climate finance, the poorest, and private money
chapters.takeaway: UK membership could help scale projects and link public money to private investment, but access to climate finance for the poorest remains a big problem.

turns.speaker: Lord Boateng
turns.text: We spend less on overseas development now. How will this subscription to UNIDO help the poorest — for example on water and sanitation — when climate money often doesn't reach them?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Our international climate finance — ICF, the money we spend on climate overseas — is smaller, so we must make it go further and mobilise other funds. Being inside UNIDO helps us scale up programmes rather than fund tiny one-offs.

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: For instance, the Brazil example showed how UK money can unlock £250 million of other public funds and attract about £2 billion of private investment — that creates jobs and local benefits.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Getting climate finance is very hard for on-the-ground projects. Is it time to change how funds are accessed and whether ODA still fits today's needs?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Yes, access is a real challenge. We work with big funds like the Green Climate Fund to speed up access. ODA — official development assistance, public development money — must now focus on mobilising private finance and building scale.

turns.speaker: Baroness Verma
turns.text: Are there rules stopping ODA working directly with private companies?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: There are constraints, but we actively use ODA to de‑risk projects and attract private capital. UK businesses are already working with UNIDO in Kenya on green tea, and on green steel in South Africa.

chapters.title: Safeguards: preventing backsliding and review plans
chapters.takeaway: The UK sees membership as a way to influence UNIDO and plans a UK-led review of the decision in 2029 to check progress.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: Organisations can slide back into bad habits. How will we stop UNIDO slipping, and will turf battles with other UN bodies be a problem?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Being a member gives us more levers to shape UNIDO and spot problems early. Many UN agencies are also undergoing broader UN reforms that should make them leaner and reduce wasteful overlap.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: Will there be a fixed review to check whether rejoining was the right move?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: Yes. The UK plans to review in 2029 whether rejoining has delivered the benefits we've set out. That review will be a UK assessment of our membership, not a UNIDO self-review.

turns.speaker: Lord Hannay of Chiswick
turns.text: Would you come back to this committee then?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: We'd expect to engage with Parliament and oversight as part of that review process.

turns.speaker: Baroness Lawlor
turns.text: Quick one: what about big partners like the US, Australia and New Zealand — are they likely to rejoin?

turns.speaker: Matt Toombs
turns.text: I won't speak for other governments. We work closely with Australia and New Zealand, and with the US where we share policy aims, but each country sets its own position.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thanks — we're short on time so we'll end this public session and move to private questions.
